analysis.one_liner: Adds a prescription drug benefit to Medicare with government-negotiated drug prices and cheaper imports from Canada.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a single vote, and Congress instead passed a Medicare drug benefit that barred the government from negotiating drug prices.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have added a voluntary prescription drug benefit to Medicare starting in 2006, with a $275 deductible, insurance covering half of drug costs up to $4,500 a year, and protection after $3,700 in out-of-pocket spending. Low-income beneficiaries would pay little or nothing. Unlike the drug bill Congress eventually passed, it would have required the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate maximum drug prices, let pharmacies and individuals import cheaper drugs from Canada, and tightened rules that brand-name drug makers use to delay generic competition. It also raised Medicare payments for rural hospitals and providers. The bill was referred to two House committees, sent to their health subcommittees in July 2003, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, especially the roughly 135%-of-poverty-and-below seniors who would get full premium subsidies and reduced cost-sharing. Seniors would also benefit from federally negotiated maximum drug prices and access to lower-priced Canadian imports. Generic drug makers, Canadian pharmacies, and rural hospitals and providers would gain financially.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors on Medicare and rural providers

how_it_helps.text: Creates a voluntary Medicare prescription drug benefit available to every Medicare beneficiary starting January 1, 2006, with a $275 deductible, 50% coverage of drug costs up to a $4,500 initial coverage limit, and cost-sharing dropping to 15% after out-of-pocket spending reaches $3,700.

Requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate contracts with drug manufacturers setting maximum prices that pharmacies may charge enrollees, and guarantees beneficiaries access to those negotiated prices even before their coverage kicks in.

Provides full premium subsidies and reduced cost-sharing for individuals with incomes below 135% of the federal poverty level, and creates a Medicare discount card program with transitional assistance for low-income beneficiaries.
Directs the Secretary to permit pharmacists, wholesalers, and individuals to import prescription drugs from Canada into the United States under specified conditions.

Limits the 30-month delay brand-name manufacturers can impose against generic competitors and provides for forfeiture of the 180-day generic exclusivity period when a first generic applicant fails to market promptly.

Raises Medicare payments to rural hospitals and providers, including equalizing urban and rural hospital payment rates, higher rural ambulance, home health, and rural clinic payments, and relief for small rural and sole community hospitals.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers would bear the largest cost, through federally negotiated maximum prices, easier generic competition, and Canadian importation. Taxpayers would fund the new benefit, which the bill caps: if projected 10-year outlays exceeded $400 billion, the Secretary would have to impose proportional cuts to beneficiary protections. Private insurers and pharmacy benefit managers would deliver the coverage but face contract standards, audits, and price pass-through disclosure.

drawbacks.text: The standard benefit left a large gap: enrollees paid all drug costs themselves once spending passed the $4,500 initial coverage limit until their own out-of-pocket costs reached $3,700, meaning a beneficiary using expensive medications would pay thousands of dollars out of pocket in the gap.

The bill contained a self-imposed spending cap: if the Secretary estimated that 10-year budget outlays would exceed $400 billion, she was required to make proportional reductions in the cost-sharing protections the benefit promised.

The benefit was delivered through private risk-bearing entities such as insurers and pharmacy benefit managers rather than directly by Medicare, adding intermediary administration, plan-by-plan formularies, and premiums that varied with plan bids, and the bill preempted state insurance standards governing those plans.

An honest supporter would also acknowledge that mandating Canadian importation and price negotiation carried real uncertainty for drug supply safety and pharmaceutical research revenue, which opponents of such provisions cited.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real coverage to uninsured seniors and meaningful tools for lowering drug prices — government negotiation, Canadian importation, and curbs on generic-delaying tactics. Its weaknesses were the coverage gap in the standard benefit and a rigid $400 billion cap that could automatically cut the promised protections if costs ran higher. It was a substantive alternative rather than a well-polished product, but its headline costs fell on an industry, not on beneficiaries.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House committees and their health subcommittees and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended; meanwhile a different Medicare drug bill, the Medicare Modernization Act of 2003, passed and became law.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Thompson introduced the bill on June 25, 2003, joined by 21 House Democrats as cosponsors; no Republicans sponsored it.
The Speaker referred it to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced.
In early July 2003 it was referred to the health subcommittees of both committees, and the record shows no further action of any kind for the rest of the 108th Congress.

The bill would have had the government negotiate maximum prescription drug prices and permitted drug importation from Canada, provisions absent from the drug benefit law Congress instead enacted in late 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead, along with the private insurers and pharmacy benefit managers who delivered the drug benefit under the law Congress passed instead — the Medicare Modernization Act of 2003 created drug coverage delivered through private plans and expressly prohibited the government from negotiating drug prices, while leaving the Canadian importation ban intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers and private insurers

for.name: Rep. Mike Thompson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Prescription Drug and Medicare Improvement Act of 2003 on June 25, 2003.

against.name: Rep. Billy Tauzin
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral of the bill on the day of introduction and never scheduled a markup or any committee action; the record shows only a July 7, 2003 subcommittee referral.

against.name: Rep. Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral of the bill on the day of introduction and never scheduled a markup or any committee action; the record shows only a July 11, 2003 subcommittee referral.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Opposed government price negotiation, Canadian drug importation, and curbs on the tactics used to delay generic competition during the 2003 Medicare drug benefit debate.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican supported it; the bill never reached a floor vote, and the competing drug benefit bill that became law in 2003 was carried by the Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill required the government to negotiate maximum prices for drugs sold to Medicare enrollees, narrowed the 30-month stay generic makers face, tightened forfeiture of the 180-day generic exclusivity period, and allowed drug importation from Canada. Each provision cuts into revenue that comes from charging Americans among the world's highest drug prices.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and health insurers
industries.note: The bill made private risk-bearing entities — including pharmacy benefit management companies and insurers — the delivery channel for the new Medicare drug benefit, locking in their intermediary role. It subjected them to federal contracts, negotiated-price pass-through, audits, and standardized appeals, so their position was preserved but regulated.
By limiting the 30-month stay against generics and providing for forfeiture of the 180-day first-filer exclusivity period when generics are delayed, the bill would speed cheaper generics to market.
The bill directed the Secretary to permit pharmacists, wholesalers, and individuals to import prescription drugs from Canada, opening a channel for Americans to buy lower-priced medicines abroad.

industries.industry: Rural hospitals and health care providers
industries.note: The bill raised Medicare payments for rural hospitals, ambulances, home health agencies, rural health clinics, and small sole community hospitals, improving the finances of rural facilities that serve patients who have few alternatives.
